extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent applicants (students, researchers, engineers) seeking guidance on responding to USPTO Office Actions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for the Office Actions and prosecution stage of a U.S. patent application: identifies types of Office Actions, deadlines, limitations after a final action, and the permitted content/strategies for responses to overcome rejections and obtain allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Action — content and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: An Office Action is an official letter from the USPTO patent examiner responding to your application. It outlines the examiner’s findings, including: Whether your invention is patentable; Any rejections or objections; Citations of prior art; Requests for clarifications, corrections, or amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Office Action to identify the legal and technical grounds for rejections and to plan a targeted response addressing each listed issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Prosecution — definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent prosecution is the back-and-forth communication between you (the applicant) and the USPTO after filing. It includes: Responding to Office Actions; Amending claims; Explaining or arguing why your invention should be patentable; Continuing examination or appealing decisions if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand prosecution as managing and negotiating your application with the examiner (note: 'prosecution' here is not criminal). Plan for iterative responses and possible appeals or continuations as part of strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑Final Office Action — characteristics and response deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: The first formal response from the examiner: lists rejections (based on prior art or legal requirements) and may include technical objections (e.g., unclear language, improper claim structure). You have 3 months to respond (extendable to 6 months with fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond within the deadline or pay extension fees. Address both substantive rejections (e.g., prior art) and technical objections (e.g., claim clarity/format) in your response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Office Action — limitations and subsequent options
rubrics_metrics.description: If your first response doesn’t resolve all issues, the examiner will issue a final rejection. You still have options, but you can’t introduce new material or make unrestricted claim changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a final action consider limited claim amendments, filing a continuing application, or appealing; avoid attempting to add new subject matter in response to a final rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted response methods and strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: You can submit a written response that may include: Amending claims (e.g., to narrow them or add details); Arguments explaining how your invention differs from cited prior art; Declarations or technical evidence; Interviews with the examiner (optional but helpful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claim amendments, clear legal and technical arguments, and evidentiary declarations where appropriate to overcome rejections. Examiner interviews can clarify issues and aid negotiation toward allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goal of prosecution responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Your goal is to overcome rejections and bring the application to allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame amendments and arguments toward patentability and allowance; prioritize resolving the examiner's stated objections and distinguishing cited prior art.
